header: Date: 2026-04-02 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Carlos Reyes (BlueLeaf CTO), Anita Sharma (BlueLeaf ML), Tom Nguyen (BlueLeaf SRE)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on real-world latency numbers for app invoke, clarifying SDK function-calling patterns, and finalizing structured-output contracts. Agreed to run dedicated-pool benchmarks, share prompt/schema artifacts, and deliver updated pilot pricing. Discussed VPC onboarding questions and fallbacks for graceful degradation.
topics: SDK usage patterns and function calling
structured JSON output schema and validation
hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs and capacity reservation
transcript: [00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — numbers, sdk patterns, schema, then next steps. we have 52 minutes. Maya on deck for perf.
[00:00:12] Carlos: Yep thanks. we just want to see where we're at for POC acceptance. latency targets are p95 < 250ms on average for the app invoke flow — that's our stretch.
[00:00:25] Maya: okay noted. we ran two permutations last week: hosted small batch and a dedicated 1-gpu pool with kv caching warmed. i'll walk through the numbers now, they might look noisy though.
[00:00:38] Anita: small note, our prompts have variable length — from one-shot to longer agent style — so distribution matters. we've attached examples in the drive link earlier.

[00:00:48] Maya: right, we used three buckets: short, medium, long. warm runs show median token latency at ~40ms per token on dedicated. end-to-end p95 for short prompts landed at ~220ms in the best run, but some spikes to 480 when cold.
[00:01:06] Tom: spikes are concerning. are those cold kv cache misses or container spinup? we need to know what's the dominating factor.
[00:01:14] Maya: a mix. we saw both KV cache cold-starts and occasional kernel schedule jitter. on hosted we saw higher variability — p95 closer to 480-600ms for same load.
[00:01:26] Jordan: so dedicated looks promising for our SLOs but we need consistent warm-state behavior — is autoscaling causing evictions?

[00:01:36] Maya: autoscale can, if policy is aggressive. for the benchmark we pinned instance counts to avoid scale churn. recommend for pilot: reserve minimal dedicated capacity or enable burst cap so you don't get evicted during peak tests.
[00:01:49] Carlos: reserve capacity is fine — what's the minimum commit you'd recommend for our traffic profile?
[00:01:55] Jordan: based on your projected qps from the telemetry you shared, we suggested a 2-GPU reservation with burst headroom. i'll include price tiers in the follow-up.

[00:02:05] Anita: on the sdk side, we're using the node SDK but hitting two issues: function-calling hooks sometimes produce extra fields and the schema validator fails. we've built a thin wrapper but want to align to Redwood's structured-output guidance.

[00:02:19] Maya: yeah we saw that — function calling returns can include assistant messages and then the function payload. if your validator is strict it will choke. recommended pattern: use the SDK's parseFunctionResponse helper and pass the expected JSON schema; also include fallback parsing for partial outputs.
[00:02:35] Tom: is there a canonical JSON schema template we should copy? the docs are a bit high level.
[00:02:40] Jordan: we can share a starter schema for the main flows — actions, metadata, and confidence scores. Anita said she'll share 3 flows; we'll iterate the schema off those.
[00:02:50] Anita: will do. also, how does batching affect ordering? we have a sequence dependency — some prompts must be atomic.

[00:02:58] Maya: batching is transparent for independent requests. for sequence-sensitive flows don't batch, or batch with per-session ordering safeguards. our SDK supports per-request metadata that preserves ordering on the server side if you tag session ids, but it's not guaranteed when you mix synchronous function-calls — so avoid batching there.
[00:03:15] Carlos: that means more tokens and cost for some flows. tradeoffs again - latency vs cost.
[00:03:20] Jordan: yup. Optimize where you can: prefix caching for common prompts, quantization profiles for the model variant, and split heavy flows into async jobs where possible.
[00:03:31] Anita: quick question on KV cache — our inference pattern reuses context a lot, can we rely on Redwood's kv cache across requests or do we need sticky sessions?

[00:03:40] Maya: kv cache is per-model-instance; with dedicated pool and pinned sessions you get persistent kv. on hosted it's ephemeral. if you need cross-request reuse without sticky routing, we can enable prefix caching at the app layer or ask you to maintain the cache client-side.
[00:03:52] Tom: ok. Also security: is the dedicated deployment compatible with our VPC and customer-managed KMS? we need to confirm key rotations and audit logs for SOC2 audit.

[00:04:01] Jordan: yes — Private/Dedicated mode supports customer VPC peering and KMS integration. we'll share the security pack and SOC2 attestation. timeline for that doc is today, i'll attach in the follow-up.
[00:04:12] Carlos: great. back to function calling: sometimes the model returns slightly malformed JSON — we need resilient deserialization. any built-in tooling?

[00:04:20] Maya: SDK has a tolerant parser and you can use the structured-output config to request 'json-strict' or 'json-tolerant' behaviors. for the POC we can run a test with 'json-tolerant' and surface parsing errors into the telemetry so you can evaluate error rates.
[00:04:36] Anita: that would help. can telemetry include raw model output samples for cases that fail schema? we want to triage quickly.
[00:04:42] Maya: yes, we can include anonymized output snippets and payload hashes in the logs. full raw output is possible in Private deployment with proper retention controls.
[00:04:53] Jordan: moving onto specific benchmark numbers from our last run — Maya?

[00:04:56] Maya: sure. short prompts (<= 64 tokens): median E2E 140-160ms on dedicated pin, p95 220-260ms. medium (64-256): median 280-320ms, p95 420-480. long (>256): median 520-640, p95 800+. on hosted the short p95 averaged 480ms. caveat: our warm-run set was primed; cold runs double in some cases.
[00:05:24] Tom: that aligns with what we saw in staging. do you have per-component breakdown — model time vs network vs parse time?
[00:05:31] Maya: yes. tokens generation time ~60% of E2E, network + parse ~30%, SDK deserialization ~10%. If you optimize parsing (native bindings) you can shave ~50ms.
[00:05:44] Jordan: for your p95 target of 250ms most short prompts on dedicated are in range but medium prompts will need either model variant with faster kernels or token limit trimming.
[00:05:54] Carlos: what's the cost delta to move to the faster model variant? and does Redwood support on-the-fly model switching for fallback?

[00:06:02] Jordan: faster model variants are typically quantized or pruned and cost less per-token; i'll include a recommendation matrix in the follow-up. Redwood's routing supports model fallback by policy — can hit cheaper variant if primary overloaded.
[00:06:14] Anita: When fallback happens, is there a deterministic difference in JSON field names or is it consistent? we rely on stable schema across variants.

[00:06:21] Maya: by design schema is independent of model variant; however output phrasing may change which can affect parsers. best practice: rely on structured function calling and explicit attributes rather than free-text parsing.
[00:06:33] Tom: about the SDK — we're seeing spiky CPU usage in our app when calling the node SDK's deserializer. is there a lower-overhead option?

[00:06:40] Maya: we have a light-weight streaming parser in beta for node that reduces memory churn; i can include a package link. also consider offloading heavy parsing to a background worker if latency critical.
[00:06:52] Carlos: any gotchas for serverless infra? we're primarily on k8s but some functions are lambda-ish.

[00:06:58] Jordan: serverless cold starts amplify model cold-starts; dedicated with pinned sessions mitigates that. for serverless consider an async job pattern or small warm pool to keep endpoints hot.

[00:07:09] Anita: quick nit: we hit a serialization mismatch where the function call included an extra underscore field _metadata and our validator rejects it, should we strip unknown properties or accept?
[00:07:18] Maya: configurable — validator can be set to 'stripUnknown' or 'failFast'. for production I'd recommend 'stripUnknown' plus telemetry to notify devs when unknown fields appear.
[00:07:28] Tom: can Redwood's console surface those schema mismatch counts?
[00:07:31] Jordan: yes, Console will show schema error counts per-route and example payloads; that's in the pilot telemetry package.
[00:07:37] Carlos: about latency benchmarks, can we replicate your dedicated run from our side? we'd like a reproducible harness so we can run nightly checks.
[00:07:44] Maya: absolutely — i'll share the benchmark harness (k6 + custom client) and the exact run parameters. you can run it in your env pointed at the reserved endpoint if we grant test creds.
[00:07:54] Anita: please make sure the harness simulates the exact token distributions, not just request sizes. our long-tail prompts matter.
[00:07:59] Maya: noted. we'll include token distribution files and the seed prompts.

[00:08:05] Jordan: let's talk timeline briefly: Anita to share prompts by monday, Maya to run benchmark and upload results by next wednesday, Jordan will send pricing and security docs by tuesday. everyone good?
[00:08:15] Carlos: yes
[00:08:16] Anita: yes
[00:08:20] Maya: quick question from our side — are there particular error budget constraints we should be aware of for the POC?
[00:08:25] Carlos: our product team set p95 < 250ms for primary flows and error rate < 0.5% for parse failures. if we exceed that we need immediate remediation.
[00:08:36] Jordan: ok we'll bake those into the acceptance checklist. Maya will instrument schema fail counts and p95 telemetry per-route.
[00:08:43] Anita: curious, do you have recommendations for retention of audit logs to satisfy our security team? they want 90 days of raw request logs with redaction.
[00:08:51] Jordan: default retention is 30 days; enterprise add-on supports 90+ days with field-level redaction and SIEM hooks. i'll include options and costs.
[00:08:59] Tom: final minor — function call timeouts. what's recommended? we saw some hung function calls at 30s and the SDK default was 60s.
[00:09:07] Maya: set server-side function timeout to 12s for interactive flows; you can set longer for batch async. 60s often indicates downstream confusion.

[00:09:15] Jordan: wrapping up — recap of what we agreed: Maya will run the dedicated benchmark and share, Jordan will send pricing + security pack, Anita will share prompts and schemas, Tom will coordinate the perf run date. we'll meet again next Thursday same time. Anything else?
[00:09:29] Carlos: nothing else from me. thanks everyone.
[00:09:33] Anita: thanks. also please include the node streaming parser link.
[00:09:36] Maya: will do, i'll paste links in the follow-up notes and attach the harness repo.
[00:09:40] Jordan: perfect. end of meeting.
